titulo.texto: Chapayeka Mask / Pharisee of the Yaqui Holy Week

frase_gancho.texto: Enormous ears and a long nose: the mask of the Pharisees of the Yaqui Holy Week.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the mask, we move on to the music of the sierra. Look for a handmade wooden violin, beside a small drum with two skin heads.

guion_corto.texto: This leather mask, with enormous ears and a long nose, belongs to a chapayeka, also called a Pharisee, a central figure of the Holy Week of the Yaqui people, or Yoeme, of Sonora. It is painted with geometric lines and crosses in red, white, and black, and tufts of horsehair or wool hang from the top. The men who wear it are fulfilling a vow, a promise, during Lent, and they dress in a blanket, a belt of hooves, and a wooden sword. They represent the persecutors of Christ and the forces of evil. On Holy Saturday, at the end of Holy Week, evil is defeated: the dancers take off their masks and throw them into the fire. It is a sacred theater in which the whole community takes part.

guion_largo.texto:
The Yaqui call themselves Yoeme, «the people». They live in southern Sonora, beside the Yaqui River, and their language belongs to the same great family as Nahuatl. They are not the same people, of course, but their languages share a very remote origin. You may remember that the Mexica told of having come from the north, from Aztlán: here in the north, sister languages of theirs are still alive.

In the seventeenth century, Jesuit missionaries arrived in the region and, with them, the Christian calendar. The Yaqui did not simply accept it: they blended it with their ideas about the wilderness, the water, and the ancestors, and created a Holy Week unlike any other. This mask is part of that blend.

For forty days, Lent turns the entire community into a stage. The Pharisees move through the streets and the church, and, as the story goes, while they wear the mask they keep silent and communicate through gestures and the noise of their belts. Putting on the mask means ceasing to be oneself. That is why it is treated with respect and not as a carnival costume.

Then comes the outcome. On Holy Saturday, amid bells and flowers, as the story goes, the Pharisees lose the battle, take off their masks, and throw them onto a bonfire. Since many masks end up in the fire, new ones must be made every year. That is why it is remarkable to have one here: normally, these objects disappear once their function is over.

Other Yaqui dancers have their place in the festivities. The Pascolas dance and make people laugh, and the deer dancer imitates the movements of the animal, from drinking in the wilderness to falling prey to the hunt. Around their legs they tie the tenábaris, the strings of cocoons filled with small pebbles that you already saw drawn on the [dancer of Tlatilco](mna_s03_bailarina_cascabeles). The deer, which appeared in the tracks of the [desert petroglyph](mna_s11_petroglifo_desierto) and in the Wixárika yarn paintings, is a sacred animal in the north.

In the Toltec Hall, you saw a warrior who wore a coyote as a helmet to take on its strength. Here the idea is different: whoever puts on the mask takes on the role of evil so that the community can defeat it. It is one of the oldest forms of theater, and it is still performed every year.

The history of the Yaqui is also one of resistance. For centuries they defended their territory and the water of the river, and in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries there were wars and deportations. According to historians, thousands of Yaqui were sent far from their land, among other destinations to the henequen haciendas of Yucatán, where you saw [the terno](mna_s19_terno_yucateco). That the festival survives is a way of returning home.

When you look at the mask, imagine the sound of the hooves on the belt striking the floor, a rhythm that announces the Pharisee. Behind this leather object lies a lesson: the community renews itself every year by remembering that evil exists and that, united, it can overcome it.

texto: Look for the enormous ears and the elongated nose
Observe the crosses and the lines painted in red, white, and black
Imagine the noise of the belt’s hooves as the wearer walks

texto.Technique/Material: Dried goat leather, kid-goat wood, natural hair, and pigments
texto.Function: Ritual masking paraphernalia for the Yaqui Lent and Holy Week

texto.pregunta: Myth: The chapayeka mask is a carnival costume.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is part of a religious vow of the Yaqui Lent, and at the end of Holy Week many masks are burned.
